messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Film Director
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 35

The accident happened eighteen months ago, on a rainy Tuesday night in February. He was driving home from a late editing session, the cut of a key scene still playing in his head, when a delivery truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan on the driver’s side. He remembers the sound—not a crash, but a deep, percussive thud like a bass drum struck too hard. Then silence, then the smell of gasoline and wet asphalt. He was trapped for nearly twenty minutes before the fire crew cut him out. He has no memory of the hospital, only of waking up three days later with a fractured pelvis, three broken ribs, and a face full of glass cuts that the plastic surgeon said would heal well. They did, mostly. But the scar along his left eyebrow catches the light differently now, and he notices it every time he looks in a mirror.

He returned to work after six months. The insurance company settled, the trucking company apologized, and the lawyers told him he could move on. He wanted to believe them. He is a film director, after all—he knows how to tell a story, how to shape chaos into narrative, how to give an audience a satisfying ending. But real life does not offer cut points. There is no fade to black when the credits roll on trauma.

Now, in the present, he avoids driving after dark. He tells his partner it’s because his eyes tire easily, which is true, but the real reason is the way his chest tightens every time he sees headlights in the rearview mirror. He takes long routes home to avoid intersections, especially the one near the editing studio. When he cannot avoid them—when a location scout forces a left turn across traffic—he holds his breath until the turn is complete, then exhales slowly, as if he has just surfaced from deep water.

On set, he has become meticulous to the point of obsession. He insists on multiple safety briefings for stunts, rechecks rigging himself, and once stopped production for an hour because a camera crane swayed too much in the wind. His crew calls him cautious; his producer calls him difficult. He knows what they don’t: that every unexpected loud noise—a dropped light stand, a slammed door—sends his heart into his throat, and that he spends the first ten minutes of every morning scanning the room for exits.

He has not told his partner about the nightmares. They come three times a week, always the same: he is driving, the truck appears, and this time there is no rescue. He wakes drenched in sweat, his hand already reaching for the passenger seat, as if to check she is still there. She sleeps through it, but he lies awake afterward, listening to her breathe, replaying the moment of impact in his mind, wondering if the intersection will ever feel safe again. Sometimes, during the day, a particular sound—the screech of tires, the clatter of a dropped metal tool—will trigger a wave of nausea and a vivid flash of the twisted dashboard. He has learned to mask it: a cough, a sudden interest in his phone, a quick turn to the window.

He still loves his work, but the joy has thinned. Where he once saw possibility in every frame, he now sees risk. The world has shrunk into a series of hazards to be managed. When a colleague asked if he was ready to direct again, he said yes. He means it. But some nights, alone in the editing suite, he freezes at the sound of a car horn from the street below, and he waits, hand on the doorframe, until his breathing steadies. He has not told anyone that.
